$description: Meta-schema for consistency_fields.json — describes the metadata properties attached to every config field and how to interpret them.
$how_to_read: Each field in consistency_fields.json carries a set of metadata properties beyond 'type' and 'description'.
This file documents what those properties mean, what values they can take, and how to use them when reading or editing the config.
Start with 'visibility' to understand WHO a field is for.
Then check 'mutability' to understand WHETHER you can safely change it.
Then check 'serialized' to understand WHETHER changing it will drift from what's already stored in the database.
Then check 'affects' to understand WHAT will be impacted by a change.
Then check 'overridable_per' to understand WHERE the override should live (global config vs. per-lens record).
Then check 'stability' to understand HOW SETTLED the field is — experimental fields may change or disappear.
Finally, read 'notes' for human context: trade-offs, edge cases, and gotchas specific to that field.
Rule of thumb: if 'mutability' is 'immutable' and 'serialized' is true, DO NOT rename or remove the field — it will orphan database records.
If 'visibility' is 'user', the value is writer-facing copy — tone and clarity matter.
If 'stability' is 'experimental', the field may change shape or be removed in a future version — don't build critical features on it yet.

visibility.purpose: Identifies the intended audience for this field's value or effect. Answers: 'Who is this for?'

user.meaning: The writer (end user) sees this field's value or its effect directly in the UI.
examples: scaffold beat labels (shown in outline preview)
user.implication: Treat as user-facing copy. Tone, clarity, and wording matter. Changes here affect what the writer reads — review for plain-language readability before shipping.

developer.meaning: A developer or admin tunes this field to control engine behaviour. Not shown to end users, but affects their experience indirectly.
examples: tunables.roles (which LLM role each pass uses)
developer.implication: Safe to change without user-facing copy review. But test the downstream effect — a role change alters quality/cost/latency.

system.meaning: Purely engine-internal. Neither the writer nor the developer needs to think about this field day-to-day — it's consumed by code only.
examples: bit_dependency (controls which bits the outline pass fetches)
system.implication: Changes here are invisible to users but can break internal contracts. Validate against code that reads the field.

visibility.how_to_read: Ask: 'If I change this value, who will notice?' If the answer is 'the writer, immediately, in the UI' → user. If 'a developer tuning the engine' → developer. If 'only the code' → system.

mutability.purpose: Describes how and when this field can be changed. Answers: 'Can I safely change this, and what does it take?'

config.meaning: Change by editing the yml file. Takes effect on next server restart or config reload.
config.implication: Safe to change freely. No migration needed. But if 'serialized' is also true, check whether existing DB records will drift from the new config value.

runtime.meaning: Can be changed via API or UI without restarting the server. Takes effect immediately.
examples: (currently no fields are runtime-mutable — reserved for future per-project settings)
runtime.implication: Changes are immediate and reversible. No restart needed.

immutable.meaning: Changing this field's value will break references in the database or in other config sections. Treat as a permanent identifier.
immutable.implication: NEVER rename or remove without a data migration. If you must change it, write a migration that updates all referencing DB rows first.

mutability.how_to_read: Ask: 'What breaks if I change this?' If nothing → config. If a restart is needed but nothing breaks → config. If DB records become orphans → immutable.

affects.purpose: Lists which system layers are impacted when this field changes. Answers: 'What will be different after I change this?'

ai_pipeline.meaning: Changes how the LLM is called — prompt construction, model selection, what context is sent, or how responses are parsed.
ai_pipeline.downstream_impact: Probe results, extraction quality, outline generation quality. May affect cost and latency.
ai_pipeline.how_to_verify: Re-run a consistency scan on a test project and compare probe outputs before/after.

ui_display.meaning: Changes what the writer sees in the frontend — labels, chart shapes, warnings, available options in pickers.
ui_display.downstream_impact: Writer experience. No data-layer or AI-layer change.
ui_display.how_to_verify: Open the consistency lab in the browser and visually inspect the affected area.

data_model.meaning: Changes how bits, scopes, or charts are structured, typed, or filtered. May change what data is produced or consumed.
data_model.downstream_impact: Existing saved data may become inconsistent with the new structure. New scans will produce different-shaped results.
data_model.how_to_verify: Check that existing DB records still load correctly. Run a fresh scan and inspect the data shape.

performance.meaning: Changes speed, cost, or resource usage of engine runs. No functional change to results.
performance.how_to_verify: Time a consistency scan before/after. Check API usage metrics.

outline_generation.meaning: Changes how the grand outline flow scaffolds or generates scene structure.
outline_generation.downstream_impact: Different outline shapes for the same synopsis. Only affects templates with grand_fit=true.
outline_generation.how_to_verify: Generate a grand outline from a test synopsis and inspect the structure.

affects.how_to_read: Read the list to understand the blast radius of a change. A field that affects only ['ui_display'] is cosmetic. A field that affects ['ai_pipeline', 'data_model'] changes both what the AI does and how results are stored — higher risk, test more thoroughly.

serialized.purpose: Whether this field's value is persisted to the database (in saved lens or chart data records). Answers: 'Will the DB and the config disagree if I change this?'

true.meaning: This field's value (or a derivative) is stored in the database when a writer saves a lens or when chart data is computed.
true.implication: If you change the config value, existing DB records will still hold the OLD value. This can cause mismatches. Either: (a) write a data migration, (b) accept that old records use old values, or (c) don't change it.

false.meaning: This field lives only in the config file. The database never stores it. Changing it takes effect cleanly on next load.
examples: template.label (re-read from config on every page load)
tunables.* (engine reads from config at scan time)
false.implication: Safe to change without worrying about DB drift. The new value takes effect everywhere immediately on reload.

serialized.how_to_read: If serialized=true AND you're changing the value: check whether a migration is needed. If serialized=false: change freely, the config is the single source of truth.

overridable_per.purpose: Whether a per-project or per-lens override can replace the global config value. Answers: 'Can different lenses use different values for this field?'

no.meaning: This field is global — all lenses and all projects use the same value from the config file.
no.implication: One value, everywhere. If you need per-lens variation, you'd need to create a separate template.

per_lens.meaning: A saved lens can override this field's value via the chart_overrides JSON column. The config value acts as the default; the override wins when present.
examples: chart.label (lens can have a custom title)
per_lens.implication: The config value is the fallback. When reading this field at runtime, code checks chart_overrides first, then falls back to config. Changes to the config only affect lenses that haven't overridden the field.

overridable_per.how_to_read: If overridable_per='per_lens': the config value is a default, not a mandate. Some saved lenses may have their own value in chart_overrides. Changing the config won't affect those lenses.

stability.purpose: How settled this field is. Answers: 'Can I rely on this field still being here and working the same way next month?'

stable.meaning: Finalized and safe to depend on. The field's name, type, and semantics are not expected to change.
stable.implication: Build features and write tests against this field confidently.

experimental.meaning: Feature-gated, partially implemented, or likely to change shape. May be removed or restructured.
experimental.implication: Don't build critical features on this field. Check the implementation status before using it. If the feature gate is off, the field has no effect.

reserved.meaning: Declared in the schema but not yet consumed by any template or code path. Placeholder for future use.
examples: bit_kinds.state.emotional (no template consumes it yet — emotional_journey is probe-only)
reserved.implication: The field exists in config but does nothing today. Don't remove it (it signals intent), but don't expect it to work either.

stability.how_to_read: If stability='stable': use freely. If 'experimental': check whether the backing code is ready before relying on it. If 'reserved': it's a placeholder — don't build on it, but don't delete it either.

notes.purpose: Free-form human context — trade-offs, edge cases, gotchas, and reasoning that don't fit into structured metadata.
notes.required_on: optional (present when the field has non-obvious behaviour)
notes.how_to_read: Read notes when you're about to change a field or when you're confused about why it exists. Notes often explain: why the default was chosen, what goes wrong at extreme values, or what other fields this one interacts with.

$reading_order.description: Recommended order for reading metadata when evaluating a config change.

steps.question: WHO is this field for?
steps.decision: If 'user': review wording as copy. If 'developer'/'system': focus on functional correctness.

steps.question: CAN I safely change this?
steps.decision: If 'immutable': stop — you need a migration plan before touching it. If 'config': proceed with a restart. If 'runtime': proceed, takes effect immediately.

steps.question: WILL the database and config disagree after I change this?
steps.decision: If true: check existing DB records. Either migrate them, accept drift, or don't change. If false: safe to change, config is the single source of truth.

steps.question: WHAT will be different?
steps.decision: Read the list to gauge blast radius. ['ui_display'] only = cosmetic, low risk. ['ai_pipeline', 'data_model'] = functional change, test thoroughly.

steps.question: WHERE does the override live?
steps.decision: If 'no': one value globally. If 'per_lens': some saved lenses may ignore your config change because they have their own override.

steps.question: HOW SETTLED is this field?
steps.decision: If 'experimental' or 'reserved': check implementation status before depending on it.

steps.question: ANYTHING ELSE I should know?
steps.decision: Read for trade-offs, edge cases, and interaction effects with other fields.

$cross_references.description: How metadata properties interact with each other — combinations that signal specific situations.

patterns.meaning: This is a database identifier. Changing it orphans stored records.
patterns.action: Write a data migration before changing. Or don't change it.

patterns.meaning: User-facing copy that lives in the config file. Changing it is safe but affects what writers read.
patterns.action: Review for plain-language clarity. No migration needed.

patterns.meaning: Engine-internal structural field. Changing it alters how data is shaped but users won't notice directly.
patterns.action: Test with a fresh scan. Check that existing data still loads.

patterns.meaning: Config value is the default, but saved lenses may have overrides. Changing config only affects lenses without overrides.
patterns.action: If you want the change to affect ALL lenses (including those with overrides), you need to clear the override from those lens records too.

patterns.meaning: Feature-gated config knob. Safe to change — nothing is stored — but the backing code may not be ready.
patterns.action: Check implementation status before flipping. If the code isn't landed, the field has no effect (or may break).

patterns.meaning: Tuning knob that trades quality for speed/cost. No user-visible change in UI, but scan times and API bills will shift.
patterns.action: Benchmark before and after. Consider A/B testing on a representative project.
